chapters.n: Zephaniah gives an unusually long family line, reaching back four generations to “Hizkiah” — likely King Hezekiah. He prophesied under King Josiah (640–609 BC), probably before Josiah’s great reforms.

f.g: His name means “Jehovah has hidden” or “Jehovah treasures” — fitting for a book about being hidden in the day of wrath (2:3).
Probably King Hezekiah of Judah (about 715–686 BC).

chapters.n: The book opens with a sweeping warning: the Lord will sweep away everything from the face of the land.

f.g: Literally “gather, gather” — sweep completely away.

chapters.n: People, animals, birds, and fish will be swept away — a reversal of Creation’s order. The idols that make people stumble will go with the wicked.

f.g: Idols or ruins — things that cause people to fall.

chapters.n: Judgment will focus on Judah and Jerusalem. God will remove every trace of Baal worship and the idolatrous priests.

f.g: Idolatrous priests (Hebrew kemarim).

chapters.n: He will cut off those who worship the stars on rooftops, and those who swear by the Lord and by Milcom at the same time — trying to serve two masters.

f.g: Milcom (or Molech), the national god of Ammon.

chapters.n: Also those who have turned away from the Lord and those who simply never bother to seek Him. Indifference is a form of rejection.

f.w: those that have not sought the LORD

chapters.n: Be silent before the Lord! His day is near. He has prepared a “sacrifice” and invited guests — but the shocking twist is that Judah itself is the sacrifice.

f.w: Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord GOD

f.g: Consecrated His guests — perhaps the invading armies.

chapters.n: On that day God will punish the officials, the royal family, and those who dress in foreign styles — a sign of adopting pagan ways.

f.g: Foreign clothing, perhaps worn in pagan worship.

chapters.n: He will punish those who leap over the threshold (a pagan superstition) and fill their masters’ houses with violence and fraud.
Cries will rise from Jerusalem’s Fish Gate, wailing from the newer Second Quarter, and crashing from the hills — the city falling district by district.

f.g: The Mishneh, or “Second Quarter,” a newer part of Jerusalem (2 Kings 22:14).

chapters.n: Wail, you who live in the market district! All the traders and money handlers will be wiped out.

f.g: “The Mortar” — a hollow market district in Jerusalem.
Literally “people of Canaan,” a term used for traders.

chapters.n: God will search Jerusalem with lamps to find the complacent — those like wine left too long on its dregs, who think, “God won’t do anything, good or bad.”

f.g: Like wine left on its sediment — thick, stagnant, complacent.

f.w: The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil

chapters.n: Their wealth will be plundered and their homes destroyed. They will build and plant but never enjoy the results — covenant curses coming true.

f.w: build houses, but not inhabit them

chapters.n: The great day of the Lord is near and coming fast. Even warriors will cry bitterly.

f.w: The great day of the LORD is near

chapters.n: A famous description: a day of wrath, distress, ruin, darkness, and clouds. The Latin hymn “Dies Irae” (“Day of Wrath”) takes its name from this verse.

f.w: That day is a day of wrath
f.g: In Latin, “Dies irae, dies illa” — the opening of a medieval hymn based on this verse.

f.w: a day of darkness and gloominess

chapters.n: A day of trumpet blasts and battle cries against fortified cities and high towers.

f.g: Walled, fortified cities.

chapters.n: People will stumble like the blind because of their sin; their lives will be treated as worthless as dust.
Silver and gold won’t save them on that day. God’s jealous fire will consume the land. Wealth cannot buy deliverance from judgment.

f.w: Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them

f.g: Zeal — God’s passionate commitment to His covenant.

chapters.n: Zephaniah calls the shameless nation of Judah to gather together — to assemble in repentance while there’s still time.

f.g: Shameless, or undesirable.
In Hebrew, a play on gathering straw or stubble — they are like chaff.

chapters.n: Do it before the decree takes effect, before the day blows away like chaff, before the Lord’s fierce anger arrives.

f.g: The husks blown away when grain is winnowed.

chapters.n: Seek the Lord, all you humble people who keep His commands. Seek righteousness and humility — perhaps you will be hidden on the day of His anger. Zephaniah’s name (“the Lord hides”) is echoed here.

f.w: Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth
it may be ye shall be hid

chapters.n: Now judgment turns to the nations, starting west with the Philistine cities. In Hebrew there are puns: Gaza (Azzah) will be abandoned (azubah), and Ekron uprooted (te‘aqer).

f.g: Pun: Azzah will be azubah (forsaken).
Pun: Eqron te‘aqer.

chapters.n: Woe to the coastal people, the Cherethites (Philistines from Crete). God will destroy Philistia completely.

f.g: A Philistine group, likely originally from Crete.

f.w: O Canaan, the land of the Philistines

chapters.n: The coast will become pastureland, with shepherds’ huts and sheep pens.

f.g: Shepherds’ shelters; perhaps also “wells” or “caves.”

chapters.n: That coastland will belong to Judah’s faithful remnant. The Lord will care for them and restore their fortunes.

f.g: Restore their fortunes; bring back the exiles.

chapters.n: Turning east: God has heard Moab and Ammon mocking His people and boasting against their borders.
God swears Moab and Ammon will become like Sodom and Gomorrah — weeds and salt pits forever. Fittingly, both nations descended from Lot, who escaped Sodom.

f.g: Salt flats near the Dead Sea — barren land.

chapters.n: This is what pride earns: they mocked and bragged against the Lord’s people.

f.w: This shall they have for their pride

chapters.n: The Lord will make all the false gods waste away, and people everywhere — even in distant coastlands — will worship Him.

f.w: famish all the gods of the earth
f.g: Starve them — idols will lose their worshipers and offerings.

f.w: all the isles of the heathen

chapters.n: To the far south: Ethiopia (Cush) too will fall by God’s sword.

f.g: Cushites, from the Nile region south of Egypt; Cushite kings had ruled Egypt.

chapters.n: To the north: God will destroy Assyria and make Nineveh a dry wasteland. Nineveh fell in 612 BC.
Wild animals and birds will roost in Nineveh’s ruins; their calls will echo through empty windows. Its fine cedar paneling will be exposed to the weather.

f.g: A wild bird — perhaps the desert owl.
Perhaps the hedgehog or a screech owl.

chapters.n: This was the proud city that felt secure and said, “I am, and there is no one else.” Now it is a den for animals, and passersby hiss and shake their fists.

f.w: I am, and there is none beside me

f.g: Gestures of scorn and horror.

chapters.n: Now Zephaniah turns back to Jerusalem itself: woe to the rebellious, defiled, oppressive city. After judging the nations, he reveals God’s own city is guilty too.

f.g: Rebellious.

chapters.n: Four failures: she didn’t listen, didn’t accept correction, didn’t trust the Lord, and didn’t draw near to God.
Her officials are like roaring lions and her judges like wolves that devour everything by morning.

f.w: they gnaw not the bones till the morrow
f.g: They leave nothing — not even bones — until morning.

chapters.n: Her prophets are reckless and unfaithful; her priests profane what is holy and twist the law.

f.g: Reckless, frivolous.

f.w: her priests have polluted the sanctuary

chapters.n: Yet the righteous Lord is right there in the city. He never does wrong; morning by morning He reveals His justice — but the unjust feel no shame.

f.w: every morning doth he bring his judgment to light

chapters.n: God has destroyed other nations and left their cities empty as a warning.

f.g: Corner towers or battlements.

chapters.n: God hoped Jerusalem would learn and fear Him so it wouldn’t be destroyed. Instead they eagerly did even more evil.

f.g: They were eager — they hurried to do wrong.

chapters.n: So “wait for me,” says the Lord, until the day He rises to gather the nations and pour out His anger. The whole earth will be consumed by His jealous fire.
Then a beautiful turn: God will give the peoples pure lips, so all can call on His name and serve Him together — a reversal of the confusion of languages at Babel.

f.g: Literally “a pure lip” — speech purified for worship.
Literally “with one shoulder” — side by side, united.

f.w: turn to the people a pure language

chapters.n: From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, God’s scattered worshipers will bring Him offerings. The gathering reaches the ends of the earth.

f.g: My scattered people.

f.w: From beyond the rivers of Ethiopia

chapters.n: On that day Jerusalem won’t be shamed by past sins, because God will remove the proud. No one will be arrogant on His holy mountain again.

f.w: thou shalt no more be haughty

chapters.n: God will leave a humble, lowly people who take refuge in the Lord’s name.
This faithful remnant will do no wrong and tell no lies. Like sheep, they will graze and rest with nothing to fear.

f.w: neither shall a deceitful tongue be found in their mouth

chapters.n: Sing, shout, rejoice with all your heart, daughter of Zion! The mood shifts from judgment to celebration.
The Lord has removed your punishment and driven out your enemy. The King of Israel — the Lord Himself — is with you. Never again fear disaster.

f.w: the king of Israel, even the LORD

chapters.n: On that day Jerusalem will hear: “Don’t be afraid; don’t let your hands hang limp.”

f.w: Let not thine hands be slack

chapters.n: A tender verse: the mighty Lord is in your midst to save you. He will delight in you with joy, quiet you with His love, and rejoice over you with singing. God sings over His people!

f.w: he will rejoice over thee with joy
he will rest in his love
f.g: Or “He will quiet you by His love” — or be silent in His love.

chapters.n: God will gather those who grieved because they couldn’t attend the sacred festivals, those who bore the shame of exile.

f.g: The appointed sacred feasts at the temple.

chapters.n: God will deal with all oppressors, save the lame, gather the outcasts, and turn their shame into praise everywhere.

The book ends with promise: God will bring His people home, gather them, and make them honored among all peoples, restoring their fortunes before their eyes. Latter-day Saints see this in the gathering of Israel.

f.w: At that time will I bring you again
